title: Planning place of birth
blurb: Give women the NICE NG235 evidence on each birth setting, for first and later babies, and support the choice they make.
question: Hannah, 29, is at low risk and expecting her first baby. She wants to give birth at home and asks how this compares with the hospital. What should the midwife tell her?

teach.h: Her choice, informed by the evidence
teach.body: Formally, NICE NG235 says women at low risk may choose any birth setting (home, freestanding midwifery unit, alongside midwifery unit or obstetric unit) and must be supported in that choice wherever they choose to give birth. In plain English: birth is generally very safe for low-risk women and their babies. Your job is to explain the trade-offs clearly, using the Birthplace data, then back her decision.

teach.body: Discuss local facts for every setting: the chance of a familiar midwife and of one-to-one care, access to obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff, birthing pools, pain relief options, and the likelihood, reasons and timing of transfer (NG235 1.3.5). Do not disclose personal views or judgements about her choice (1.3.11). If either of you wants more discussion, involve a senior or consultant midwife, and an obstetrician if there are obstetric issues (1.3.10).

teach.caption: Discuss the risks and the extra care an obstetric unit can give so she makes an informed choice (1.3.9).

teach.h: Scenario: Hannah plans a home birth
teach.body: Midwife Tom explains that for a first baby, planning birth at home means fewer interventions than an obstetric unit, but about 9 per 1,000 babies have a serious medical problem compared with about 5 per 1,000 in other settings. About 45% of first-time mothers planning home birth transfer, most often for delay in labour. Hannah decides to stay with her home birth plan; Tom supports her, records her choices and plans how transfer would work.

teach.text: The small increase in risk to the baby applies to a FIRST baby planned at HOME. For multiparous women at low risk, NICE says there is no difference in outcome for the baby in any setting. Higher BMI, especially above 35, is a reason to discuss setting, not an automatic bar (1.3.6).

items: Low-risk women may choose any setting and must be supported in that choice.
Midwifery units: fewer interventions, no difference for the baby, for first and later babies.
First baby at home: fewer interventions, but about 4 more serious problems per 1,000 babies; about 45% transfer.
Tables 6-7 suggest the obstetric unit; tables 8-9 mean individual assessment.
Give local facts, keep personal views out, escalate discussion to a senior midwife if needed.

summary: You can now explain the NG235 place-of-birth evidence separately for first and later babies, including intervention, transfer and baby outcome figures. You can also use the risk tables to guide individual discussion and support a woman's informed choice.

A.q: Rosa is having her third baby and is at low risk. She asks whether planning a home birth affects the outcome for her baby compared with an obstetric unit. What does NICE NG235 say?
options: There is no difference in outcome for the baby
There is a small increase in adverse outcomes
The baby has a better outcome at home
The risk of a serious problem roughly doubles
A.why: NG235 1.3.3 and 1.3.7: for low-risk multiparous women, planning birth at home or in a midwifery-led unit is associated with fewer interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby.

whyNot.1: The small increase applies to nulliparous women planning a home birth.
whyNot.2: NICE reports no difference for the baby, not a better outcome.
whyNot.3: Rates of serious problems were about 3 per 1,000 in both settings.

A.q: For low-risk nulliparous women who plan a home birth, roughly what proportion transfer to an obstetric unit?
options: About 10%
About 25%
About 45%
About 70%
A.why: NG235 table 4: 450 per 1,000 nulliparous women planning home birth transfer to an obstetric unit.

whyNot.0: About 10% is closer to the multiparous home-birth figure (115 per 1,000).

A.q: Which condition in NG235 table 6 suggests planned birth in an obstetric unit?
options: Sickle cell trait
Age 40 or over at booking
Confirmed cardiac disease
Thalassaemia trait
A.why: Confirmed cardiac disease is in table 6, medical conditions indicating increased risk and suggesting planned birth at an obstetric unit.

whyNot.0: Sickle cell trait is in table 8: individual assessment needed.
whyNot.1: Age 40 or over is in table 9: a factor to take into account.
whyNot.3: Thalassaemia trait is in table 8: individual assessment needed.

B.q: According to Birthplace data quoted in NG235, what is the most common main reason for transfer from home to an obstetric unit?
options: Request for regional analgesia
Abnormal fetal heart rate
Retained placenta
Delay in the first or second stage
B.why: Delay during the first or second stage of labour accounted for 32.4% of transfers from home, the largest single reason.

whyNot.0: Requests for regional analgesia accounted for 5.1% of transfers from home.
whyNot.1: Abnormal fetal heart rate accounted for 7.0% from home.
whyNot.2: Retained placenta accounted for 7.0% from home.

B.q: While discussing place of birth, Chloe asks her midwife, 'Would you have your baby at home?' Which response best follows NICE NG235?
options: Share her own birth experience to help Chloe decide
Advise the obstetric unit as the safest choice for all
Decline to discuss place of birth until 36 weeks
Explain the evidence without giving personal views
B.why: NG235 1.3.11: when discussing a woman's choice of place of birth, do not disclose personal views or judgements about her choices.

whyNot.0: Personal experience is a personal view and may bias her decision.
whyNot.1: This is a judgement that misstates the evidence for low-risk women.
whyNot.2: Choices should be discussed as early as possible in pregnancy.

B.q: Sana, a multiparous woman at low risk with a booking BMI of 38, would like to give birth in a freestanding midwifery unit. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell her midwifery units do not accept a BMI over 35
Discuss BMI-related risks and how quickly help can be reached
Advise a home birth instead, as transfer is quicker
Book her for the obstetric unit without further discussion
B.why: NG235 1.3.6: higher BMI, particularly above 35, increases the likelihood of complications, and advanced care can generally be given more quickly in an obstetric or alongside unit. Discuss this so she can decide.

whyNot.0: NICE asks for discussion, not a blanket BMI exclusion.
whyNot.2: Advanced care is generally quicker in an OU or AMU than at home.
whyNot.3: Booking without discussion removes her informed choice.

C.q: Hannah, nulliparous and at low risk, wants to plan a home birth. Which summary of the NG235 evidence should the midwife give?
options: Fewer interventions, but a small increase in risk for the baby
Outcomes for the baby that match every other birth setting
A higher caesarean rate than planning an obstetric unit birth
No difference in intervention rates between birth settings
C.why: NG235 1.3.3 and 1.3.8: planning home birth for a first baby is linked with fewer interventions but an overall small increase (about 4 more per 1,000) in serious medical problems for the baby.

whyNot.1: That applies to midwifery units, not home, for nulliparous women.
whyNot.2: Unplanned caesarean was lower at home (80 per 1,000) than in an OU (121).
whyNot.3: Interventions were clearly higher in the obstetric unit.

C.q: Ama is multiparous; her last baby weighed 4.7 kg. She wants to give birth in the alongside midwifery unit. How should NICE's tables guide the midwife?
options: It is in table 7, so advise the obstetric unit
It is a table 9 factor, so assess her individually
It rules out midwifery units for this pregnancy
It has no bearing on choosing a place of birth
C.why: A previous baby over 4.5 kg is in table 9: not in itself a reason for obstetric unit birth, but further consideration of setting is needed.

whyNot.0: Table 7 lists factors suggesting OU birth; a previous large baby is in table 9.
whyNot.2: Table 9 factors call for individual assessment, not exclusion.
whyNot.3: It is listed precisely because it needs discussion.

C.q: Freya, who had a caesarean in her last pregnancy, wants to plan birth in a freestanding midwifery unit. She and her midwife both want further discussion. Who should be involved?
options: The GP who referred her at booking
The health visitor who will see her
A senior midwife and an obstetrician
The neonatal team on the labour ward
C.why: NG235 1.3.10: arrange discussion with an appropriately trained senior or consultant midwife, and a senior or consultant obstetrician if there are obstetric issues, as previous caesarean is.

whyNot.0: The GP is not the professional NICE names for this discussion.
whyNot.1: Health visitors do not plan intrapartum care.
whyNot.3: Neonatal input may be useful but does not address her obstetric risk.

reteach.title: Two women, two answers
reteach.question: Why does NICE give a first-time mother and a mother of three a different answer about home birth?

blocks.body: For a woman having a later baby at low risk, every setting gives the baby the same outcome, and home or a midwifery unit means fewer interventions. For a first baby, midwifery units still match the obstetric unit for the baby with fewer interventions, but home carries a small extra risk for the baby (about 9 versus 5 per 1,000) and almost half transfer.

blocks.h: Outcome for the baby vs obstetric unit

blocks.text: Fewer interventions does not equal the same outcome for the baby. For a first baby at home, both are true: fewer interventions and a small increase in risk to the baby.

explain.body: Explain that birth is generally very safe for low-risk women and babies (1.3.1). Women may choose any setting and should be supported wherever they give birth (1.3.3). All four settings should be available locally or nearby (1.2.1).

test.q: A low-risk woman chooses a setting her midwife would not have chosen. What does NICE NG235 expect of the midwife?
options: Support her in the setting she chooses
Ask her to sign a disclaimer form
Refer her for an obstetric opinion
Encourage her to reconsider each visit
test.why: NG235 1.3.3: support women in their choice of setting wherever they choose to give birth.

whyNot.1: NICE does not require a disclaimer for an informed choice.
whyNot.2: A low-risk woman's choice does not need obstetric review.
whyNot.3: Repeated pressure undermines her informed choice.

explain.body: Nulliparous, low risk: home or FMU has the highest spontaneous vaginal birth rates; the OU has the most interventions; no difference for the baby between AMU, FMU and OU; home has about 4 more serious problems per 1,000. Transfer: home 450, FMU 363, AMU 402 per 1,000.

test.q: For low-risk nulliparous women, where is unplanned caesarean birth most common?
options: Planned home birth
Freestanding midwifery unit
Alongside midwifery unit
Obstetric unit
test.why: NG235 table 4: unplanned caesarean birth was 121 per 1,000 in the obstetric unit, compared with 69 to 80 in other settings.

whyNot.0: Home: 80 per 1,000, lower than the obstetric unit.
whyNot.2: AMU: 76 per 1,000, lower than the obstetric unit.

explain.body: Multiparous, low risk: spontaneous vaginal birth 984 per 1,000 at home vs 927 in an OU; unplanned caesarean 7 vs 35; no difference for the baby in any setting. Transfer from home is about 115 per 1,000.

test.q: Which statement about low-risk multiparous women is correct according to NG235?
options: Planned home birth has a higher caesarean rate
Transfer from home happens in about 45% of cases
Obstetric units have the fewest episiotomies
Outcomes for the baby are the same in all settings
test.why: NG235 1.3.7: there are no differences in outcomes for the baby associated with planning birth in any setting for low-risk multiparous women.

whyNot.0: Unplanned caesarean was 7 per 1,000 at home versus 35 in the OU.
whyNot.1: About 45% is the nulliparous figure; multiparous is about 12%.
whyNot.2: Episiotomy was highest in the obstetric unit (56 vs 15 per 1,000 at home).

explain.body: Tables 6-7: conditions and factors suggesting planned OU birth (e.g. cardiac disease, previous caesarean, multiple birth). Tables 8-9: individual assessment (e.g. sickle cell trait, BMI, age 40+, previous baby over 4.5 kg). Higher BMI, especially over 35, raises the chance of complications (1.3.6).

test.q: Which factor is listed in NG235 table 7 as suggesting planned birth in an obstetric unit?
options: Previous caesarean birth
Grand multiparity (parity 4 or more)
Recreational drug use
Fibroids
test.why: Table 7 includes previous caesarean birth among previous complications suggesting planned obstetric unit birth.

whyNot.1: Grand multiparity is in table 9: individual assessment.
whyNot.2: Recreational drug use is in table 9 (substance misuse is in table 7).
whyNot.3: Fibroids are in table 9: individual assessment.
